facts.text: Long before email, the @ sign was used by Italian merchants in the 1500s, mainly for units of weight.
In 1971, Ray Tomlinson, an engineer at a Boston firm working on ARPANET, created an early form of email between computers.
Tomlinson needed a mark to separate a user's name from the name of the user's computer, and he chose @.
He picked @ because it was not commonly used in computing at the time and it reads naturally as at.
The & sign comes from et, the Latin word for and; it joins the letters e and t into one shape.
In the early 1800s, schoolchildren ended the alphabet with the & sign, saying and per se and, meaning and by itself and.
The phrase and per se and ran together over time and became the word ampersand.
Before hashtags, the # symbol was known as the number sign or pound sign.
On August 23, 2007, Chris Messina suggested on Twitter using the # sign to group posts on the same topic.
In fall 2007, a fire in San Diego County led to the first widespread use of a hashtag to track updates.
The power symbol combines two numerals: the line stands for 1, meaning on, and the circle stands for 0, meaning off.
The power symbol has existed since 1973, when it was included in a standard of the International Electrotechnical Commission.
The symbol was first meant for standby mode; a 2004 IEEE standard gave it the general meaning of power.
For the first Earth Day in 1970, the Container Corporation of America, a maker of paper boxes, held a contest for a recycling logo.
Design students across the United States were invited to create a logo for recycled paper.
The winner was Gary Anderson, a senior at the University of Southern California.
His design has three arrows that curve and bend back on themselves to form a continuous loop.
On September 19, 1982, Scott Fahlman of Carnegie Mellon University proposed :-) on a computer science online bulletin board.
Readers of the board often missed that some posts were jokes and took them seriously; :-) was meant to mark posts that were not serious.
The smiley is meant to be read sideways; seen that way, :-) looks like a smiling face.
